title: No eye, no ear
hookLine: in emptiness no eye, no ear, even no four truths as fixed things: the list itself held lightly
last: NOT BORN — NO BIRTH, NO DEATH.

lines: A GROCERY LIST. A PILOT'S CHECKLIST.
cards: Grocery lists. Packing lists. The checklist a pilot runs before takeoff.
Lists are wonderful: they carry what memory can't. But you've probably met someone who holds a list too tightly. The trip where the plan mattered more than the people.

The recipe followed so exactly that nobody noticed the soup was too salty. Buddhism is full of lists: four truths, five heaps, eight steps on the path, twelve links. Today the Heart Sutra does something startling.
It picks up Buddhism's own lists, one by one, and says no.

teach.b: Here's the passage, in plain words. In emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, no consciousness: the five heaps, what a person is made of.
No eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind; no sights, no sounds, no smells, all the way through: the senses and their objects.
No ignorance and no end of ignorance, all the way to no old age and death and no end of old age and death: the twelve links of dependent arising.
Then no suffering, no cause of suffering, no ending, no path: the four noble truths themselves. No wisdom and no attaining. Why would a Buddhist text say no to the four truths?
Not to throw them away. Mahayana teachers still teach these lists. The no means none of them is a fixed thing standing on its own.

Each is a way of seeing, a tool. Some scholars read the passage as a gentle pushback on earlier schools that had catalogued the building blocks of experience in great detail and treated them as the bedrock of reality.
There's an older picture for the same idea, in a sutta the Theravada tradition also keeps.
The Buddha compares his teaching to a raft. You build it to cross a river. Once across, you don't carry it on your head through the forest.
The raft was real, and it worked.
Holding it lightly is how you keep walking.

how: In Zen and other Mahayana communities the long run of 'no' lines is chanted briskly as part of the daily Heart Sutra, while the same lists (the five heaps, the four truths) are still taught in study and sermons.

o: even the senses aren't fixed things standing alone
a call to close your eyes and shut out the world
a teaching that the senses are illusions to escape

games.q: match each 'no' to the list it comes from.

s: the Heart Sutra tells Buddhists to throw out the four noble truths
Mahayana Buddhists still teach them; the 'no' says they aren't fixed things standing alone.
the sutra also says 'no wisdom and no attaining'
it doesn't exempt even wisdom from the list.
the raft picture comes from a sutta the Theravada tradition keeps
the Buddha compares his teaching to a raft for crossing, not for carrying on your head.

games.q: you've crossed a river on a raft you built yourself. it was hard work and it held. what does the Buddha's picture suggest you do now?
o: carry it on your head, in case.
burn it, since it was never real.
leave it on the bank and keep walking.
games.why: the raft worked and was real; the point is not to carry it once it has done its job.

practice: Pick one list you carry, today's to-dos, rules for yourself, a list of what's wrong, hold it in mind for a breath, then set it down beside you like a raft on the riverbank; it's still there for later. Then just listen.
When a sound comes and a label forms, car, voice, fridge, let the label go and stay with the hearing itself.

wordCard.voice: No eye. In emptiness, the Heart Sutra says, even the senses and the four truths aren't fixed things. The lists are tools.

orig.note: Sanskrit 'na cakṣuḥ': no eye. The Heart Sutra runs through eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind.

carryVoice: Your line: hold lists lightly. A raft is for crossing, not for carrying. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita-hrdaya), 'in emptiness there is no form…'
